blocks.text: Anencephaly is associated with severe abnormalities in the base of the skull (basichondrocranium), affecting its shape, position, and ossification.

**Anencephaly: Neurulation failure:** Anencephaly occurs when the neural tube fuses in the spinal cord (Caudal neuropore) but fails to fuse in the brain region (Cranial neuropore), leading to missing parts of the brain and skull.
The cranial and caudal neuropores close around day 25 and 28 of development respectively in a normally developing fetus.
Types of Neural Tube Defects:

rows: Failure of neural tube fusion in the brain region, results in missing parts of the brain and skull.
Complete failure of the neural tube to fuse, affecting both the brain and spinal cord.
Incomplete fusion of the spinal neural tube or failure of formation of vertebral arches leads to defects in the spinal cord.

blocks.text: **Malformation of the vertebral arches (Option A):** This is characteristic of spina bifida, not anencephaly.
**Herniation of brain tissue through the skull (Option C):** This describes encephalocele, a different neural tube defect, not anencephaly.
**Fusion of the cranial sutures (Option D):** This refers to craniosynostosis, which is not related to anencephaly.
This option correctly identifies the extent of exposure associated with each condition, with craniorachischisis being more severe and involving both structures.

rows: A type of spina bifida where a portion of the spinal cord remains open.

Occurs due to the failure of fusion of both the cranial as well as the caudal portions of the neural tube. (Option D)

blocks.text: Diagram

Meningocele involves only the protrusion of the meninges, not the spinal cord. When the spinal cord is also involved, the condition is called myelomeningocele. Spina bifida is a birth defect where the neural tube fails to close properly, affecting the caudal portion of the spinal neural tube.
Types:

rows:
Involves a visible sac or cyst containing the spinal cord or nerves protruding from the back.
Two types:
Meningocele: A sac containing only the meninges and CSF, with the spinal cord intact.
Myelomeningocele: Sac contains both the meninges and a portion of the spinal cord; the most severe form.
The defect is hidden under the skin, typically found in the lumbosacral or sacral regions; it affects ~5% of the population.

blocks.text: Impact on Spinal Cord Development:

rows: The conus medullaris normally ascends relative to the vertebral column. In spina bifida, this ascent is impaired, leading to a tethered cord.
The spinal cord is anchored at the defect site, restricting normal upward movement, which can cause neurological complications.
An extremely rare condition where the spinal cord is split into two columns by a bony or cartilaginous spur, often associated with tethered cord. (Option C)

blocks.text: Prenatal Diagnosis:
**Detection:** Spina bifida can be identified through ultrasound imaging during pregnancy.
Spina Bifida Occulta

items.text: **Indicator:** The posterior ossification centres of the vertebrae may display an abnormal U or V shape. (Option A)
**Incidence:** The prevalence of severe types, such as myelomeningocele, has decreased due to improved prenatal diagnosis and options for termination. (Option D)

blocks.text: Hemispatial neglect is not typically associated with agenesis of the corpus callosum. Hemispatial neglect is often seen in patients with damage to one hemisphere, particularly the right hemisphere, leading to inattention to the opposite side of space (usually the left). In agenesis, both hemispheres may function independently, so hemispatial neglect is not a hallmark of this condition.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a rare congenital condition in which the corpus callosum, the structure connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, fails to develop properly or is absent. This can lead to a range of neurological and developmental issues.
Causes:

items.text: **Genetic:** Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., trisomy 13, 18) or mutations in specific genes.
**Environmental:** Prenatal factors like infections, alcohol, or drug exposure.

blocks.text: Clinical Features:

items.text: **Developmental delays:** Intellectual disability, motor delays, and speech impairments.
**Seizures:** Common due to lack of communication between brain hemispheres.
**Motor problems:** Coordination issues, ataxia.
**Behavioral issues:** Hyperactivity, impulsivity, and autistic-like behaviors.
**Cognitive challenges:** Attention deficits and difficulty with higher cognitive functions.

blocks.text: **Associated Conditions:** Aicardi syndrome, Andermann syndrome, holoprosencephaly, fetal alcohol syndrome.
Anterior choroidal artery syndrome is associated with the clinical triad of contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral hemisensory loss and contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Anterior Choroidal Artery Syndrome
**Cause:** Infarction in the anterior choroidal artery territory.

**Pathophysiology:** AChA anastomoses with posterior choroidal artery and posterior cerebral artery. Infarction occurs in the posterior limb of the internal capsule due to a lack of collateral supply.
Complete syndrome triad:

items.text: **Contralateral hemiplegia** - Weakness or paralysis on one side of the body opposite to brain injury. (Option A)
**Contralateral hemisensory loss** - Loss of sensation on one side of the body opposite to brain injury.
**Contralateral homonymous hemianopia** - Loss of the same visual field (either right or left) in both eyes, opposite to the side of brain damage. (Options C and D)

blocks.text: Homonymous quadruple sectoranopia if the lateral geniculate body is involved. Incongruent homonymous hemianopia if the optic tract is involved.
**Neuropsychological associations:** Left neglect syndrome in right-sided lesions. Language disorders in left-sided lesions.
The corpus callosum is the largest commissure of the brain.
It is divided from before backwards into the following four parts:

items.text: **Genu:** This is the thick, curved front part of the corpus callosum, located about 4 cm behind the front of the brain. Its fibers curve forward into the front parts of the frontal lobes, forming a fork-like shape known as the forceps minor.
**Rostrum:** The genu extends downward and backward as a thin extension called the rostrum, which connects to the lamina terminalis.
**Body:** It is the central part of the corpus callosum, situated between the front (genu) and back (splenium) parts.
**Splenium:** The splenium is the large, back part of the corpus callosum, located about 6 cm in front of the occipital region.

blocks.text: Its fibers connect the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes of both brain hemispheres. The fibers connecting the occipital lobes form another fork-like shape known as the forceps major.
**Function:** The corpus callosum is largely responsible for interhemispheric transfer of information which is essential for bilateral responses and learning processes.
Lesions in the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus are known to lead to uncontrolled appetite and extreme obesity, as this area is critical for satiety and regulating food intake.

rows: Anterior Hypothalamic Area & Preoptic Area (Option A)

Can disrupt thermoregulation and lead to hyperthermia.
Mediates sympathetic responses (e.g., increases blood pressure, accelerates heart rate, cold regulation).
May cause impaired sympathetic responses and issues with stress response.
Acts as the hunger & thirst centre; stimulates food intake.
Leads to anorexia and significant weight loss.
Acts as the satiety centre; inhibits eating.
Causes uncontrolled appetite and extreme obesity.
Secretes vasopressin and oxytocin; regulates water balance and reproductive functions.
Can disrupt water balance and lead to diabetes insipidus.
Regulates circadian rhythms and biological clocks.
Can disrupt sleep-wake cycles and lead to insomnia.

blocks.text: The Ventral Posteromedial Nucleus receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways which are responsible for processing sensory information from the face.

items.text: **Ventral Anterior Nucleus:** Connects to the reticular formation, substantia nigra, corpus striatum, and premotor cortex Influences motor cortex activities. (Option A)
**Ventral Lateral Nucleus:** Similar connections to the ventral anterior nucleus. Receives input from the cerebellum and red nucleus (Option B): Projects to motor and premotor areas. (Option D)
**Ventral Posterior Nucleus:** Subdivided into:
**Ventral Posteromedial Nucleus:** Receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways.
**Ventral Posterolateral Nucleus:** Receives sensory tracts; projects to primary somatic sensory areas in the postcentral gyrus (BA 1, 2, 3)

blocks.text: Anterior Thalamic Nuclei are directly connected to the limbic system and play a crucial role in emotional tone and mechanisms of recent memory.
Thalamic Nuclei:

rows: Contains anterior thalamic nuclei. Receives mammillothalamic tract from mammillary nuclei. Reciprocal connections with cingulate gyrus and hypothalamus. Functions related to the limbic system. Concerned with emotional tone and recent memory. It is a part of the Papez circuit

Contains the large dorsomedial nucleus and smaller nuclei. Two-way connections with prefrontal cortex and hypothalamic nuclei. Interconnected with all other thalamic nuclei. Responsible for integrating sensory (somatic, visceral, olfactory) information with emotional and subjective states. (Option C)

Subdivided into dorsal and ventral tiers.
Dorsal Tier: Includes lateral dorsal nucleus, lateral posterior nucleus, and pulvinar. Interconnections with other thalamic nuclei, parietal lobe, cingulate gyrus, occipital, and temporal lobes.
Ventral Tier: Nuclei arranged in a craniocaudal sequence Further divided into ventral anterior, ventral posterior and ventral lateral nuclei

blocks.text: Other Thalamic Nuclei

items.text: **Intralaminar Nuclei:** Influence consciousness and alertness; receive input from the reticular formation.
**Midline Nuclei:** Functions unclear; receive afferent fibres from the reticular formation.
**Reticular Nucleus:** Regulates thalamic activity; connects to other thalamic nuclei.

blocks.text: **Medial Geniculate Body:** Processes auditory information; projects to the auditory cortex. (Option A)

blocks.text: **Spinothalamic tract (Option C):** This tract is responsible for transmitting pain and temperature sensations from the body to the brain. It does not pass through the genu of the internal capsule.
**Medial lemniscus (Option D):** This tract carries proprioception and vibration sense from the body to the brain, passing through the brainstem, not the genu of the internal capsule.
The corticonuclear tract, which contains motor fibres to cranial nerve motor nuclei, specifically passes through the genu of the internal capsule.
Tracts Passing Through Internal Capsule:

items.text: **Genu:** Corticonuclear tract (motor fibres to cranial nerve motor nuclei).

**Posterior Limb:** Corticospinal tract (motor fibres to the contralateral spinal cord) (Option A). Corticopontine fibres from the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes. Fibres for the upper limb (anteriorly) and trunk/lower limbs (posteriorly).
**Superior Thalamic Peduncle (through anterior and posterior limbs):** From ventral posterior and lateral posterior thalamic nuclei to parietal cortex (sensory areas).

blocks.text: Sulci of the Cerebrum

items.text: **Lateral Sulcus:** Seen laterally; separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. (Option A)
**Central Sulcus:** Runs Antero-inferiorly; separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe; visible laterally and medially.
**Calcarine Sulcus:** Visible medially; located in the occipital lobe, associated with the visual cortex. (Option C)
**Parieto-occipital Sulcus:** Seen medially; separates the parietal and occipital lobes. (Option D)

blocks.text: Lateral View Medial View
**Central Sulcus:** Divides the frontal lobe (anterior) from the parietal lobe (posterior).
**Lateral Sulcus:** Distinguishes the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.

items.text: **Pre-central Gyrus:** Located in front of the central sulcus; it contains the frontal motor cortex, which controls skeletal muscles.
**Post-central Gyrus:** Located behind the central sulcus; houses the parietal sensory cortex for general sensations (touch, pain, temperature, proprioception).
**Insula:** Found in the floor of the lateral sulcus.
**Central Sulcus:** Separates the frontal motor cortex (pre-central gyrus) from the parietal sensory cortex.
**Paracentral Lobule:** Controls the contralateral lower limb, pelvis, and perineum.
**Calcarine Sulcus:** Associated with the occipital visual cortex.
**Limbic Lobe:** Involved in emotions and memory.
**Cingulate Gyrus:** An arch-shaped convolution above the corpus callosum.

blocks.text: Cerebral Cortex Layers and Functions
Has six layers of neurons.

rows: Receives nonspecific input signals from lower brain centers. Control the excitability of stimulated areas.
Receives nonspecific input and sends axons to the opposite cortex through the corpus callosum.

Sends axons to related cortical areas on the opposite side through the corpus callosum. The outer band of Baillarger is a part of this layer of cerebral cortex, specifically located in the motor cortex and somatosensory cortex.
The primary layer for receiving input sensory signals, which then spread to the surface and deeper layers.
Sends large axons to distant nervous system parts like basal ganglia, brain stem, and spinal cord. Controls signal transmission.
Sends axons to the thalamus. Regulates excitability of incoming sensory signals.

blocks.text: The internal capsule is positioned medially next to both the thalamus and the caudate nucleus.
Internal Capsule

The internal capsule is a compact bundle of projection fibres that connects the cerebral cortex with subcortical centres such as the thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord. It contains both afferent (sensory) fibres from the thalamus to the cortex and efferent (motor) fibres from the cortex to the cerebral peduncle and midbrain.
Relations of Internal Capsule

items.text: **Medially:** Thalamus and caudate nucleus
**Laterally:** Lentiform nucleus
**Anterior limb:** Between the head of the caudate nucleus and the anterior part of the lentiform nucleus (Option A)
**Posterior limb:** Between the thalamus and the posterior part of the lentiform nucleus.
**Genu:** Bend between the anterior and posterior limbs, concave laterally (Option B)
**Retrolentiform part:** Behind the lentiform nucleus (Option D)
**Sublentiform part:** Below the lentiform nucleus.
